guide.title: Kent, Connecticut: Iron Furnaces and a Covered Bridge
guide.intro: Kent was incorporated in 1739 in Connecticut's northwest corner, on land sectioned in 1737 and settled two years later, taking its name from the county of Kent in England. Once a thriving iron-ore producer and farming community, the town is rural and residential today, its historic neighborhoods — Flanders, the Cobble, and Bulls Bridge — still carrying those names. Bull's Bridge, the covered bridge over the Housatonic River, was built in 1842 using architect Ithiel Town's patented lattice-truss design and once carried a major highway between Hartford and Newburgh, New York. The Schaghticoke Indian Reservation lies within Kent's borders, and Native Americans fished and camped at what is now Kent Falls in an area they called "Scatacook." In 1969 the Stanley Works tool company donated the building that became the Eric Sloane Museum, set beside the ruins of the old Kent Iron Furnace.

sections.heading: Iron ore, a furnace, and Seven Hearths
sections.body: By the mid-1700s Kent's iron deposits had built a real industry, and the ruins beside today's Eric Sloane Museum are what remain of the Kent Iron Furnace, now listed on the National Register of Historic Places and designated a State Archaeological Preserve. In the Flanders District, Seven Hearths — built in 1751 by John Beebe, Jr. and notably larger than its neighbors at 32 by 52 feet — survives as the Kent Historical Society's museum. Downriver, Bull's Bridge still carries traffic on a single lane over the Housatonic gorge, one of only two Connecticut covered bridges still open to cars.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: Kent sits on US Route 7 in Connecticut's northwest hills, about 28 miles north of Danbury and 25 miles south of North Canaan, with CT Route 341 running east 8 miles to Warren. There's no rail station in Kent itself — the nearest is Dover Plains, New York, west on Metro-North's Harlem Line, with service toward Grand Central Terminal.

sections.heading: Falls, a farm brewery, and Main Street
sections.body: Kent Falls State Park's main cascade drops about 70 feet as part of a series of falls descending 250 feet toward the Housatonic, with a covered bridge and an art trail reproducing 19th-century landscape paintings at the entrance. On Main Street, the Fife 'n Drum has been Kent's dining and lodging hub for decades, with tableside flambes, a 7,000-bottle wine cellar, and rooms popular with families visiting Kent's private schools; Kent Falls Brewing Company pours flights at its working farm on Camps Road.

faq.question: How do I get to Kent?
faq.answer: By car via US Route 7 — about 28 miles north of Danbury or 25 miles south of North Canaan — or CT Route 341 from Warren, 8 miles east. There's no rail station in Kent; the nearest is Dover Plains, NY, west on Metro-North's Harlem Line toward Grand Central Terminal.

faq.question: What is Bull's Bridge?
faq.answer: A covered bridge over the Housatonic River built in 1842 with architect Ithiel Town's patented lattice-truss design. It's one of only two Connecticut covered bridges still open to motor vehicles, restricted to a single lane.

faq.question: What is the Eric Sloane Museum?
faq.answer: A museum of artist and author Eric Sloane's paintings and early-American hand-tool collection, with the Noah Blake Cabin and the ruins of the Kent Iron Furnace on the grounds. It's a seasonal state museum — check current hours before visiting.

faq.question: Is Kent Falls State Park free?
faq.answer: Yes, though there's a parking fee: free for Connecticut-registered vehicles, $10-15 for out-of-state vehicles. The park is open daily, 8 a.m. to sunset.

faq.question: Where can I eat and stay in Kent?
faq.answer: The Fife 'n Drum Restaurant and its adjoining inn anchor Main Street, with Kingsley Tavern and Kent Falls Brewing Company nearby. Bull's Bridge Inn overlooks the covered bridge itself. The Kent Collection's Victorian is a boutique bed-and-breakfast near the village center.

places.name: Kent Falls State Park
places.summary: A series of cascades descending 250 feet toward the Housatonic, with a roughly 70-foot main falls, a covered bridge, and the 'Viewpoints' Art Trail reproducing 19th-century landscape paintings. Open daily, 8 a.m. to sunset; free for Connecticut-registered vehicles, $10-15 for out-of-state.

photos.title: Kent Falls State Park
photos.description: The lower cascades of Kent Falls, part of the series of falls descending toward the Housatonic River.
photos.author: Neil Gundel

places.name: Eric Sloane Museum
places.summary: Paintings and the early-American hand-tool collection of artist and author Eric Sloane (1905-1985), plus the Noah Blake Cabin from his book 'Diary of an Early American Boy'; the grounds hold the ruins of the Kent Iron Furnace. A seasonal state museum with limited hours — check before visiting.

places.name: Connecticut Antique Machinery Association Museum
places.summary: An all-volunteer, 8-acre campus dedicated to preserving, restoring, and demonstrating antique industrial and agricultural machinery, next to the Eric Sloane Museum. No regular public hours — open during its dated 2026 shows, such as the spring Powerup Show and fall festival.

places.name: Seven Hearths Museum (Kent Historical Society)
places.summary: A colonial residence built in 1751 by John Beebe, Jr. in the Flanders District, notably larger than earlier homes there at 32 by 52 feet. The Kent Historical Society opens it by seasonal guided tour, May through September, and by appointment.

places.name: Bull's Bridge
places.address: Off US Route 7 at the Housatonic River, Kent, CT (Bulls Bridge district)
places.summary: Built in 1842 with Ithiel Town's patented lattice-truss design, one of only two Connecticut covered bridges still open to motor vehicles, carrying a single lane of traffic over the Housatonic gorge.

photos.title: Bull's Bridge over the Housatonic River
photos.description: The weathered covered bridge at Bull's Bridge, framed by autumn foliage above the Housatonic gorge.
photos.author: Bob P. B.

places.name: Fife 'n Drum Restaurant
places.summary: Longtime hub of Kent, noted by Yankee Magazine for tableside flambes and a 7,000-bottle wine cellar, with live piano Friday, Saturday, and Sunday evenings. Closed Tuesdays.

places.name: Kent Falls Brewing Company
places.summary: A working-farm brewery with a tasting room offering flights, petite pours, and bottles and cans to go, with afternoon hours most days.

places.name: Kingsley Tavern
places.summary: Main Street tavern featured in The New York Times, with dinner Tuesday-Thursday and Friday, and brunch and dinner Saturday. Closed Sunday and Monday.

places.name: Bull's Bridge Inn
places.summary: A 200-plus-year-old building overlooking Bull's Bridge and the Housatonic gorge, serving aged steaks and seafood; voted best 'Family Dining in Litchfield County' by Connecticut Magazine. Dinner-only on weekdays, with weekend brunch.

places.name: Fife 'n Drum Inn
places.summary: Ten named guest rooms above and beside the landmark Fife 'n Drum Restaurant in the center of Kent village, popular with families visiting Kent's three private schools. Booking by phone or email.

places.name: The Kent Collection — The Victorian
places.summary: A boutique property built in 1890 and fully renovated in 2022, bookable room-by-room or as a full house, within a quarter mile of Kent's restaurants and galleries.

links.note: Both northwest-corner towns built their economies on 18th-19th century iron ore and furnaces.
Kent and Salisbury both mined iron ore and ran furnaces in Connecticut's northwest corner.
